categories.title: Exhibition
categories.description: Available works from the guided list, in list order.

exhibits.title: Crush, Crumble & Chomp cracktro
exhibits.description: One of the earliest surviving examples of what would become the demoscene. The cracked game was modified to display "BROKEN BY THE PIRATE 09/26/81" before launching. It was basically digital graffiti: "I cracked this." Those signatures gradually became animated, musical and increasingly elaborate - and eventually separated from the games altogether.

exhibits.title: Red Sector Megademo
exhibits.description: A defining example of the megademo era: many effects, screens, tunes and coders collected into one production. The Amiga's custom graphics and audio hardware turned demos into audiovisual shows rather than decorated loading screens. Scene veterans routinely cite the Red Sector megademo as one of the productions that established the Amiga demo tradition.

guide.text: Red Sector Inc.'s 1989 Megademo shows the Amiga demoscene moving beyond simple crack intros into full audiovisual productions. Here you can see early real-time 3D, vector objects and particle-like effects that were impressive on an Amiga 500-class machine. The soundtrack uses the Amiga's four-channel sampled-audio hardware.

exhibits.title: Mental Hangover
exhibits.description: A major step toward the modern trackmo: instead of choosing separate demo parts from menus, effects flowed continuously to music as one directed presentation. It won the Swedish Elite Easter Conference 1990 and became one of the canonical early Amiga demos.

guide.text: Only a year later, Scoopex's Mental Hangover shows a major jump in both 3D complexity and presentation. Instead of a collection of separate demo screens, effects flow continuously into one another, with more elaborate rotating objects, calculated transformations and bitmap graphics integrated into the sequence. Mental Hangover helped establish the trackmo format: a continuously streaming, directed demo rather than a menu of independent parts.

exhibits.title: Jesus on E's
exhibits.description: The demoscene collides head-on with early-90s rave culture. A roughly 27-minute, two-disk audiovisual assault using techno/rave samples, rapidly changing effects and synchronized graphics. It feels closer to a VJ set than a traditional computer demo and remains one of the weirdest, most unmistakably early-90s productions. Released 24 October 1992.

guide.text: Jesus on E's takes a very different direction. Instead of treating music as accompaniment to graphical effects, the production is essentially a 27-minute rave audiovisual show, with rapidly changing real-time graphics synchronized to a continuous techno soundtrack. Released in 1992, it shows how the demoscene was absorbing contemporary rave, sampling and VJ culture.

exhibits.title: State of the Art
exhibits.description: Probably the most immediately recognizable Amiga demo. Rotoscoped human dancers, bold typography and abstract graphics were synchronized tightly to music instead of focusing purely on technical flexing. It won the Amiga demo competition at The Party 1992 and strongly pushed the scene toward graphic design, editing and music-video aesthetics.

guide.text: State of the Art became one of the most famous Amiga demos of the era. Spaceballs recorded real dancers, traced their movement and converted it into animated graphical silhouettes, then synchronized them tightly to techno music. Combined with bold typography, geometric patterns and concentric animated rings, it made the demo feel more like a music video than a traditional technical showcase. In 1992, producing this fluid animation in real time required aggressive use of the Amiga's graphics hardware.

exhibits.title: Desert Dream
exhibits.description: A huge, cinematic two-disk Amiga production combining 3D, elaborate transitions, graphics and Laxity's soundtrack. It represents the peak of the classic Amiga epic demo style: long, technically dense and unapologetically grandiose.

guide.text: By 1993, Kefrens' Desert Dream shows the classic Amiga demo reaching a much more cinematic scale. Real-time 3D scenes, dot landscapes and tunnels are mixed with carefully drawn bitmap artwork, transitions and synchronized music. Rather than demonstrating one isolated effect, the production uses 3D as part of a longer visual narrative.

exhibits.description: Representative of the late-90s shift from "look at our new graphics routine" toward design, rhythm and audiovisual direction. It won the X 1997 PC demo competition and became a classic of the more stylistically sophisticated post-Second Reality generation.

guide.text: By 1997, PC demos such as Acme's 303 could manipulate far more complex real-time 3D surfaces. Here, reflective-looking materials, distortion and continuously transforming geometry demonstrate the transition from simple polygon demonstrations toward full software-rendered visual environments. 303 also puts much greater emphasis on design, editing and synchronization rather than showing effects in isolation.

exhibits.title: Heaven Seven
exhibits.description: A complete audiovisual production - including 3D, textures, animation and music - inside 65,536 bytes. Its polished ray-traced visual style made the size limit almost unbelievable and helped establish the 64K intro as one of the scene's premier art forms. It won the Mekka & Symposium 2000 64K competition.

guide.text: Heaven Seven demonstrates a completely different kind of technical constraint. This entire 2000 production - executable code, generated graphics, animation and music - fits within a 64-kilobyte intro. Most strikingly, it performs real-time ray tracing, calculating lighting, reflections and 3D imagery while the demo runs. Effects that normally required pre-rendered CGI were now being generated live inside an executable smaller than many single image files.

exhibits.title: fr-08: .the .product
exhibits.description: One of the biggest technical turning points in demoscene history. Farbrausch built procedural content-generation tools and a real-time software synthesizer, allowing a substantial 3D world plus soundtrack to fit into 64 KB. Its techniques and tools heavily influenced the following decade of size-limited demos.
